questions.explain: The chapter defines a page as 8 KB with a 96-byte header, data rows, and a slot array (row-offset array) at the end; rows are addressed through the slot array, not by byte offset, so free space can be compacted without invalidating references.
options: A 24-byte header and rows addressed by byte offset
Data rows first, then a variable-length header
A 96-byte page header, data rows growing downward, and a slot array growing up from the end of the page
A 64 KB header followed by eight page descriptors
questions.q: What is the internal layout of a SQL Server 8 KB data page?

questions.explain: PFS records how full each page is (in five buckets), GAM/SGAM track which extents are free or in use, and IAM records which extents belong to which object — so finding free space is a metadata lookup, never a scan.
options: They store user data overflow from the heap
They are the allocation metadata layer that lets the engine find free space via metadata lookups instead of scans
They encrypt data pages before writing them
They track deadlock graphs across sessions
questions.q: What role do the PFS, GAM, SGAM, and IAM pages play?

questions.explain: The chapter says every nonclustered index stores the clustering key as its row locator, so a wide clustering key bloats every index on the table.
options: A wide clustering key bloats every nonclustered index, because each one stores the clustering key as its row locator
It makes ALTER INDEX REBUILD impossible
It forces the table to be stored as a heap
It disables columnstore compression
questions.q: Why is a wide clustering key dangerous in SQL Server, according to the chapter?

questions.explain: Columnstore stores each column's values contiguously, so a SUM over ten million rows reads only that column's data and can use aggressive compression on similar values.
options: It reads whole pages so that no column is skipped
It stores each column's values contiguously, so analytical queries read only the columns they use
It requires every query to use the columnstore path
It eliminates the need for rowgroups
questions.q: Why is columnar storage (SQL Server columnstore) fundamentally better for analytical queries than row storage?

questions.explain: The chapter says fill factor only applies at index build/rebuild time (e.g., FILLFACTOR = 80 leaves 20% of leaf pages empty), while everyday inserts still fill pages toward 100% between maintenance windows.
options: Fill factor applies only at index build or rebuild time; everyday inserts still fill pages toward 100%
Fill factor reserves space permanently and inserts never exceed it
Fill factor is ignored for clustered indexes
Fill factor works only on heaps
questions.q: What is a common misconception about fill factor that the chapter corrects?
